planting.note: Plant tubers 2 inches deep after the last frost once soil has warmed, in humus-rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained woodland soil; lift and store tubers over winter north of zone 7.

directions: This East Asian subspecies of hardy begonia is distinguished from the typical form by narrower, more angular leaf lobes and leaf undersides that flush noticeably red along the veins, giving the foliage extra contrast in a shaded border. Nodding sprays of pale pink flowers open from midsummer into fall atop succulent, translucent stems, and tiny axillary bulbils drop to the soil each autumn to form new plants the following spring. It is generally considered slightly less reliably winter-hardy than the typical subspecies, so gardeners north of zone 7 should mulch heavily or lift tubers for winter storage. Grow alongside ferns and hostas in moist, humus-rich shade where it will slowly naturalize into an informal colony.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in part to full shade; mulch over winter in zone 7 where hardiness is marginal.

directions: Native to moist forest floors in central China, this rhizomatous species is grown for its deeply palmate, lobed leaves that fan out like a duck's foot or a dissected maple leaf, held on fuzzy, reddish petioles. Loose clusters of pale pink flowers rise above the foliage in summer, but the architectural leaf shape is the main draw in a shaded woodland planting. The creeping rhizome spreads slowly at the soil surface to form a textured groundcover patch over several seasons rather than a single clump. It is grown primarily by begonia specialists and shade-garden collectors rather than mainstream retail, and benefits from a protective winter mulch at the colder end of its range.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, terrarium subject, or shaded container plant in zone 9 and colder; it cannot tolerate frost. Keep in a shallow, wide pot to suit the shallow rhizome, with the top inch of substrate allowed to dry between waterings and high humidity to prevent leaf edge browning.

directions: Native to limestone forest understories in Guangxi, China, this compact rhizomatous species carries deep olive-brown, densely velvety leaves marked with a pale yellow-green star radiating out from the leaf center, a pattern distinct from most rex-type hybrids. Small white to pale pink flowers appear in loose clusters above the foliage, though the plant is grown almost entirely for its fuzzy, richly colored leaves. It spreads slowly via a surface rhizome, making it well suited to shallow pots, terrariums, and bright-shade windowsills rather than open garden beds. In mild, humid climates it can also be grown outdoors as a shaded groundcover, but it has no meaningful frost tolerance and should be treated as a houseplant elsewhere.

planting.note: Grow in a container in bright shade in zone 9 and colder, moving outdoors for summer and indoors once nights cool; it cannot tolerate frost. Use a free-draining mix and let the surface dry between waterings, especially during its winter semi-dormant rest.

directions: Native to the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal regions of South Africa, this semi-succulent species develops a swollen, caudex-like base and a slightly woody stem over time, topped with deeply lobed, maple-shaped leaves marked with reddish veining. Small white flowers appear intermittently through the warmer months, but the sculptural, drought-tolerant growth habit and attractive foliage are the main appeal. It prefers bright, filtered shade rather than deep shade and tolerates brief dry spells better than most begonias thanks to its water-storing stem base. Begonia dregei is also one of the parents of the older Begonia x weltoniensis hybrids once popular as summer bedding and container plants. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows and protect from any frost.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container specimen in zone 9 and colder; it has little frost tolerance. Use a shallow pot to accommodate the surface-creeping rhizome and keep humidity elevated for best leaf color.

directions: Collected from forested limestone hills near Dali (historically romanized 'Tali') in Yunnan, China, this rhizomatous species produces rounded, puckered leaves marked with dark patterning that traces the main veins against a lighter green background. Clusters of small pink flowers rise above the foliage in the growing season, though the patterned leaves are the main ornamental feature. Like many Yunnan rhizomatous begonias, it is grown chiefly by species-begonia collectors in shallow pots or terrariums rather than as a mainstream bedding plant. Keep it out of direct sun, which quickly bleaches the leaf pattern, and provide consistent humidity for the best foliage display.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; mulch heavily over winter at the colder end of its range in zone 8.

directions: Native to low- and mid-elevation forests of Taiwan, this rhizomatous species forms a slowly spreading groundcover of glossy, pointed leaves with reddish veining and toothed margins. Loose sprays of pale pink to white flowers appear above the foliage during the warm season, adding soft color without overwhelming the leaf display. It is somewhat more cold-tolerant than most rhizomatous begonias, with the surface rhizomes surviving light freezes under a protective mulch at the warmer end of zone 8. Grow it in consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil alongside ferns and hostas, where it slowly knits together into an attractive shaded groundcover patch.
